title: Neuro-Symbolic AI: Why the Next Real Step Isn't a Bigger Model
excerpt: Deep learning sees patterns; symbolic systems follow rules. Neither alone is enough for reliable reasoning. A practical look at why hybrid neuro-symbolic systems, from AlphaGeometry to tool-using LLMs, are quietly solving problems that pure scaling cannot.
content:
# Neuro-Symbolic AI: Why the Next Real Step Isn't a Bigger Model

For most of the last decade, progress in AI had one simple recipe: more data, more parameters, more compute. It worked far better than anyone had a right to expect. But if you have spent real time with these models, you have also felt the ceiling. A system writes a working REST API and then insists that 9.11 is larger than 9.9. It summarises a research paper and quietly invents a citation that does not exist. The pattern-matching is extraordinary. The *reasoning* is not reliable.

Neuro-symbolic AI is the most serious attempt to fix that, and it is older and more practical than the recent wave of hype suggests.

## Two halves of one brain

There have always been two cultures in AI.

The **symbolic** tradition, sometimes called GOFAI ("good old-fashioned AI"), represents knowledge explicitly: rules, logic, graphs, programs. Tell it that all humans are mortal and that Socrates is human, and it can prove that Socrates is mortal, showing you every step on the way. Symbolic systems are precise, interpretable, and verifiable. Their weakness is that they are brittle. They do not learn from raw, messy data, and they fall apart the moment reality stops matching the schema.

The **connectionist** tradition, neural networks, does the opposite. It learns directly from examples, handles noise and ambiguity gracefully, and scales beautifully. That is the engine behind modern vision and language. Its weakness is the mirror image of the symbolic one: no explicit notion of a rule, no guarantee of consistency, no built-in way to explain *why*. It interpolates. Push it past the distribution it was trained on and it does not fail loudly; it confabulates with total confidence.

Neuro-symbolic AI is the bet that these are not rival religions but two halves of one brain. You want the perception and learning of neural networks **and** the structure and guarantees of symbols, working in a single system.

## A map of the territory

The phrase covers a surprisingly wide range of architectures. Henry Kautz gave the field a useful taxonomy in his 2020 AAAI lecture, "The Third AI Summer," laying out six distinct ways to combine the two paradigms ([AI Magazine](https://doi.org/10.1002/aaai.12036)). You do not need all six, but three patterns capture most working systems:

- **Neural in, symbolic out.** A neural network handles perception, then hands clean symbols to a reasoning engine. A vision model turns an image into objects and relations, and a logic program queries them.
- **Symbolic skeleton, neural muscle.** A classical search or planning algorithm provides the backbone, and a neural network supplies the expensive intuition: which move looks promising, which branch is worth exploring.
- **Neural engine that calls symbolic tools.** A learned model decides *when* to invoke an exact external procedure, a calculator, a database, a theorem prover, and folds the result back into its answer.

The interesting part is that the most impressive recent systems built this way are not research toys. They are concrete, and they win.

## Three systems that actually work

**AlphaGo and AlphaZero.** The system that beat Lee Sedol was already neuro-symbolic, even if nobody marketed it with that word. Monte Carlo Tree Search is a textbook symbolic search procedure; the neural networks simply told the search where to look and how good a position was. Neither component could have done it alone. Search without intuition is too slow; intuition without search is too shallow.

**The Neuro-Symbolic Concept Learner.** A 2019 system from MIT and IBM answered questions about images by splitting the job in two: a neural network perceived objects and their attributes, and a symbolic program executor ran the actual logic of the question, such as "how many red cubes are left of the sphere?" ([Mao et al., ICLR 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12584)). Because the reasoning stayed symbolic, the system generalised to new question types from very little data, and you could read off exactly what it did.

**AlphaGeometry.** This is the example I point to when someone tells me symbols are dead. In 2024, DeepMind published a system that solves International Mathematical Olympiad geometry problems at close to gold-medalist level ([Nature, 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06747-5); [DeepMind write-up](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/alphageometry-an-olympiad-level-ai-system-for-geometry/)). The architecture is unapologetically hybrid: a symbolic deduction engine grinds through everything that follows logically from the diagram, and when it stalls, a language model proposes a clever auxiliary construction, the creative leap that pure logic search cannot find efficiently. Language model for intuition, symbolic engine for proof. The proofs it outputs are checkable, line by line. You do not get that from a chatbot, however large.

## LLMs are already drifting toward symbols

Here is the part people miss. The most popular fix for LLM unreliability is itself a quiet neuro-symbolic move. The moment you let a model call a Python interpreter, run a SQL query, or hand a sub-problem to a real solver, you have built a system where the neural part handles language and intent and an exact symbolic part handles the steps that must be correct.

Asking a model to do long arithmetic in its head is asking the wrong organ to do the job. Letting it write and run code is letting the symbolic half do what it is good at. Retrieval-augmented generation is the same idea applied to facts: keep the knowledge in an external, inspectable store instead of smearing it across billions of weights. The next post on this blog, on the "reversal curse," is a sharp argument for exactly why you should be careful trusting those weights as a database.

## Why this is genuinely hard

I do not want to sell a clean story. Stitching the two paradigms together runs into a real wall: neural networks live in a smooth, differentiable, continuous world, and symbols are discrete. Gradient descent does not flow naturally through a hard logical decision. A large fraction of neuro-symbolic research is, underneath, a fight over how to make discrete reasoning differentiable enough to train end to end without losing the guarantees that made symbols attractive in the first place.

And when you do bolt on a symbolic component, you can re-import its old brittleness. A reasoning engine is only as good as the symbols it receives. If the neural front-end mislabels the scene, the logic will reason flawlessly about the wrong world.

So this is not a solved problem. It is a direction, and the evidence that the direction is right keeps arriving as systems that do things scaling alone has not delivered.

## Why I care about this

My own research is on detecting hallucinations in multi-document summarization: working out when a generated summary asserts something the sources never actually support. The most promising angle is not "train a bigger judge." It is to extract structured claims from the text and check them against structured evidence, a small symbolic consistency layer sitting on top of a neural generator. That is neuro-symbolic thinking in miniature, and it is why I think this is one of the most practical corners of AI to be working in right now.

The lesson I keep returning to is unglamorous. We do not need one architecture that does everything. We need to stop asking a single mechanism to be both a poet and an accountant.

## Further reading

- Henry Kautz, [The Third AI Summer](https://doi.org/10.1002/aaai.12036) (AAAI 2020 lecture) — the taxonomy this post leans on.
- Garcez and Lamb, [Neurosymbolic AI: The 3rd Wave](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.05876) (2020).
- Mao et al., [The Neuro-Symbolic Concept Learner](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12584) (ICLR 2019).
- Trinh et al., [Solving olympiad geometry without human demonstrations](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06747-5) (Nature, 2024) — AlphaGeometry.
- Gary Marcus, [The Next Decade in AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06177) (2020) — the strongest case that scaling alone is not enough.

title: The Reversal Curse: Your LLM Knows "A is B" but Not "B is A"
excerpt: Train a model that Tom Cruise's mother is Mary Lee Pfeiffer, and it still struggles to say who her son is. A 2023 finding shows large language models store facts in one direction only, and it says something deep about what knowing even means for a transformer.
content:
# The Reversal Curse: Your LLM Knows "A is B" but Not "B is A"

Here is a result that sounds like a typo and is not. Train a language model on the sentence "Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman to travel to space," and it will happily complete that sentence. Then ask it "Who was the first woman to travel to space?" and it can fail. Same fact. Same model. One direction works, the other does not.

This is the **reversal curse**, described by Berglund and colleagues in a 2023 paper with one of the more honest titles in recent machine learning: "LLMs trained on 'A is B' fail to learn 'B is A'" ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12288)). I think it is one of the most important things a working developer can understand about these systems, because it quietly contradicts the mental model almost everyone carries around.

## The mental model it breaks

Most people, including engineers who should know better, imagine an LLM as a kind of compressed encyclopedia: facts go in, and you can look them up from any angle, the way you would query a knowledge graph. If the graph has an edge connecting Tom Cruise to his mother Mary Lee Pfeiffer, you expect to walk that edge in either direction.

The reversal curse says that intuition is wrong. The model does not store a symmetric fact. It stores a *direction*.

## The clean experiment

The strength of the paper is that it does not rely on anecdotes. The authors built a controlled test. They invented fictitious people and facts, for example stating that a made-up person named "Daphne Barrington" directed a made-up film called "A Journey Through Time," so there was zero contamination from anything the model saw during pretraining. They fine-tuned models on these facts in one direction, "[name] is [description]," then tested the reverse, "[description] is [name]."

In the reverse direction the models scored close to zero. Not "worse." Effectively chance. And when the researchers measured the probability the model assigned to the correct name, it was no higher than for a random name. The information was simply not retrievable that way. It was not buried or hard to reach; for the reverse query it may as well not have been there.

## The Tom Cruise test

The part that sent the paper around the internet was the real-world version. The authors asked GPT-4 about roughly a thousand celebrities and their parents. Ask "Who is Tom Cruise's mother?" and it answers correctly; the paper reports about 79% accuracy across the set. Then flip the question to "Who is Mary Lee Pfeiffer's son?" and accuracy collapses to around 33%.

The model demonstrably contains the connection. It just stored it pointing one way, because the text it learned from almost always mentions the famous person first and the parent second.

## Why this happens

Once you see the cause it stops being mysterious and starts being obvious, which is the best kind of result.

An autoregressive language model is trained to predict the next token given the tokens before it. When it sees "A is B," every gradient update nudges it to make B more likely *after* A. Nothing in that objective ever touches the probability of A appearing after B. There is no symmetry constraint, no rule that says if A relates to B then B relates to A. Logical symmetry is something humans impose on facts; the training objective has no idea it exists.

So the weights end up encoding an association that runs from the A-context to the B-token, and that association does not run backwards for free. "Knowing" a fact, for a transformer, means having seen it in a particular order often enough.

## What it actually means

A few consequences worth sitting with:

- **An LLM is not a database.** It is a directional, associative memory. Treating its weights as a queryable knowledge store is a category error, and the reversal curse is the cleanest proof of that.
- **Data order is a feature, not a detail.** If your fine-tuning data only ever states a relationship one way, your model will only know it one way. Teams shipping domain-tuned models on internal documents hit this constantly without ever naming it.
- **It partly explains certain hallucinations.** Asked to retrieve a fact "from the wrong side," a model does not return nothing. It returns its most fluent guess. A confident wrong answer is often exactly that.

This is also, to me, a strong argument for the neuro-symbolic and retrieval ideas in the [previous post](/blog/neuro-symbolic-ai-the-case-for-hybrid-minds). If a fact lives in an external store, a real knowledge base or a search index, you can look it up from any direction, because the structure is explicit instead of baked into one-way weights.

## Can it be fixed?

Partly. The most direct mitigation is almost embarrassingly simple: show the model both directions. Augment the training data so every "A is B" is paired with a "B is A." A 2024 follow-up named reverse training formalised this, duplicating the corpus, reversing token order in the copy, and training on both, and reported that it substantially reduces the curse ([Golovneva et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13799)). Related work by Allen-Zhu and Li on how models store and manipulate knowledge found the same underlying difficulty: models are poor at retrieving knowledge in any order other than the one they were trained on ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14402)).

None of these is a clean cure, because the problem is baked into the objective itself. They are workarounds, and good ones, but the fact that we need them is the whole point.

## If this got you curious

The reversal curse belongs to a small family of findings that reveal how strange the inside of these models really is. Three I would send you toward next:

- **Grokking** — networks that look like they only memorised, and then, long after training accuracy has hit 100%, suddenly snap into genuine generalisation ([Power et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02177)).
- **Induction heads** — the specific attention mechanism researchers traced as a key origin of in-context learning ([Olsson et al., 2022](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html)).
- **Knowledge manipulation** — the broader study of what models can and cannot do with the facts they hold ([Allen-Zhu and Li, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14402)).

The common thread is that "the model knows X" hides an enormous amount of work in that one word, *knows*. The reversal curse is the simplest place to watch it come apart.

## Sources

- Berglund et al., [The Reversal Curse: LLMs trained on 'A is B' fail to learn 'B is A'](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12288) (2023).
- Golovneva et al., [Reverse Training to Nurse the Reversal Curse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13799) (2024).
- Allen-Zhu and Li, [Physics of Language Models: Part 3.2, Knowledge Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14402) (2023).
- Power et al., [Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02177) (2022).
- Olsson et al., [In-context Learning and Induction Heads](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html) (Anthropic, 2022).

title: Building Complete Legal Aid for Production
excerpt: Lessons from shipping a legal technology platform with role-based dashboards, real-time messaging, and AI drafting workflows.
content:
# Building Complete Legal Aid for Production

Complete Legal Aid is a legal technology platform where citizens, lawyers, and admins collaborate in one system.

## My Role

I worked as Frontend Lead and Full-Stack Contributor.

## What I Built

- Full frontend experience for 3 user roles
- Real-time chat interface with attachments and read receipts
- Booking and payment UI flows
- AI drafting integration for legal document assistance

## Core Stack

- React 19 + TypeScript + Vite
- Django + WebSocket
- Firebase notifications
- GCP-backed deployment services

## Key Outcome

The AI drafting flow reduced document preparation time from around 45 minutes to under 3 minutes.

## Takeaway

In legal-tech products, workflow clarity matters as much as raw features. Reliable role separation and communication flow made the platform usable in real scenarios.

title: ChefMate: NLP + ML Pipeline from User Input to Recipe
excerpt: How I used spaCy, fuzzy matching, and scikit-learn to build a practical recipe recommendation workflow.
content:
# ChefMate: NLP + ML Pipeline from User Input to Recipe

ChefMate is an AI-powered recipe suggestion app I built as a solo developer.

## Problem

Ingredient input is usually messy: spelling errors, synonyms, and inconsistent naming.

## Pipeline

1. Normalize ingredients with spaCy
2. Handle input variation with FuzzyWuzzy
3. Predict cuisine and recipe candidates with scikit-learn
4. Return filtered suggestions through a Flask app

## Dataset

I trained models using a 643MB recipe dataset and focused heavily on preprocessing quality.

## Result

The NLP + fuzzy matching pipeline improved ingredient recognition by around 70% on noisy input scenarios.

## Takeaway

For practical ML products, input normalization often drives quality more than model complexity.

title: Care Companion: Designing an AI + IoT Healthcare Rover
excerpt: Software architecture notes from building a Raspberry Pi + Arduino healthcare monitoring rover with real-time vision.
content:
# Care Companion: Designing an AI + IoT Healthcare Rover

Care Companion combines AI and IoT for home-care monitoring.

## My Scope

I implemented all software modules and led the team workflow.

## Software Modules

- Sensor data collection pipeline
- Voice command handling
- Motor control logic
- Flask dashboard for caregiver monitoring
- OpenCV + MobileNetSSD vision inference

## Hardware Integration

- Raspberry Pi 4 as AI core
- Arduino for sensor communication
- DHT11, MQ-2, pulse, and flame sensors

## Measured Result

Real-time human detection ran at around 60 FPS on Raspberry Pi 4 during testing.

## Takeaway

Stable embedded software boundaries (sensing, control, dashboard, vision) are essential for reliable AI + IoT systems.
